/FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
Issued at 239 PM MDT Wed Sep 16 2026

Friday will be another active and potentially wet day, as we remain 
under southwesterly flow that will provide us with another push of 
monsoonal moisture from Baja California. As a result, PWAT values 
will be above the 90th percentile with a vigorous closed 500 mb low 
located over Eastern Oregon and Western Idaho. The question will be, 
will we have enough mid and upper-level forcing for ascent to 
translate most (or any?) of this moisture to the surface as 
precipitation? Ensemble guidance shows a series of low-amplitude 
shortwave troughs embedded in the SW flow regime combined with weak 
isentropic ascent/warm advection primarily over SE Wyoming, which 
would favor another round of showers and thunderstorms Friday 
afternoon and evening. Any showers and thunderstorms will be capable 
of producing heavy rainfall and even some localized flooding, hence 
WPC placing much of SE Wyoming and the extreme W Nebraska Panhandle 
in a marginal risk for excessive rainfall given the anomalously 
moist air mass. High resolution guidance also hints at somewhat of a 
stationary front draped across the I-80 corridor late Friday 
afternoon, which may serve as an additional focal point for showers 
and thunderstorms. Not expecting storm motion to be an issue in 
regards to flooding, as cloud-layer mean winds are progged to be 25-
30 knots which will keep storms moving fast enough. However, any 
backbuilding convection will pose a flooding threat, as cloud-layer 
mean wind vectors are oriented at roughly a 25 to 45 degree angle 
relative to the stationary front (so not parallel, but also not 
perpendicular to the boundary). While not an ideal flash flooding 
setup, some degree of backbuilding may occur especially if 
convection remains anchored to the aforementioned stationary 
front/boundary given the very moist airmass (PWAT 0.9"-1.1") for 
this time of year. Highs on Friday will depend on cloud cover and 
precipitation coverage. Current LREF guidance has a median high 
temperature for Cheyenne in the mid 70s, however I wouldn't be 
surprised to see this trend cooler over time, especially depending 
on convective debris and coverage of overnight showers/storms on 
Thursday into Friday morning, in additional to the exact placement 
of the stationary front. 

Heading into Saturday, ensemble guidance has backed off on shunting 
off our supply of monsoonal moisture as the closed low to our 
northwest begins to lift to the north and east. While not as 
impressive as the previous couple of days, PWAT values are still 
expected to range between the 85th and 95th percentiles relative to 
climatology, keeping additional shower and thunderstorm chances in 
the forecast. The bulk of the forcing for ascent looks to be from 
late Saturday evening into the overnight hours, with an additional 
chance for some much needed rainfall. As it stands, ensemble 
guidance has 55-65% chances of all areas east of the I-25 corridor 
seeing at least 0.1" of rain from midnight to noon on Sunday, with 
the highest values across the Nebraska Panhandle. However the spread 
remains rather large, with the 25th percentile QPF being essentially 
0.01"-0.05", which wouldn't exactly do much to help our drought 
conditions. Forecast soundings across the Panhandle show skinny CAPE 
profiles throughout the troposphere, PWAT values around the 70th 
percentile, and warm cloud layers up to ~3 km, so any showers and 
storms are expected to be rather efficient rainfall producers. 
Unsurprisingly, high temperatures on Sunday will be rather cool 
(although not terribly far below average) in the 60s for SE Wyoming, 
and low 70s in the Panhandle. 

Heading into the work week, a warming trend is expected as flow is 
more out of the WNW, resulting in drier conditions as another ridge 
builds to our west over the Great Basin. Expect temperatures to be 
around or slightly above seasonal values on Monday and Tuesday in the 
upper 60s to mid 70s (warmest temps across the Panhandle), and 
little to no chances for precipitation. 

On Wednesday, ensemble guidance hints at the ridge building and 
shifting east, placing SE Wyoming and W Nebraska in more WSW flow 
aloft, allowing for some return of monsoonal moisture. At this time, 
any monsoonal moisture surge doesn't look nearly as impressive as 
the one in the short/medium range, but low precipitation chances look 
to return come mid next week.
